newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadians banned from seeing polls before vote.
newsitem.headline: Canadians banned from seeing polls before vote.

text.p: Canadians will cast their votes for a new federal government in a general election on Monday, but they will be banned from seeing any opinion polls after Friday.

The country's electoral law bans 72 hours before an election the publication of any type of poll -- including informal "hamburger" polls, in which restaurants sell burgers named after the party leaders. The candidate with the most hamburgers sold in his name, wins.
The polling blackout rule is being challenged before the Supreme Court of Canada, but the court will not hear the case until after the June 2 election.
In the midst of the information explosion in North America, the ban on polls has infuriated the Canadian media.

"Be warned: If you order a Big Mac Manning (hamburger) tomorrow, you may go to prison," Globe and Mail columnist Andre Picard wrote on Friday, referring to Reform Party leader Preston Manning. "Dare utter the Pope's real name -- he's a Pole -- and off you go to the big house."
The blackout includes any communication about previous polls already published as well as exit polls on election night.
Canadian law also has strict rules for the media on election day.

"The Canada Elections Act makes it an offense for anyone to publish, by any means, election results in an electoral district in which the polls have not closed," Elections Canada, the nation's electoral authority said in a news release.
In a country with six time zones, complying with the law is no easy feat.
Elections Canada tried to coordinate the closing of the polls across the country so that all Canadians would learn the outcome of the election at about the same time.
However, the Prairie province of Saskatchewan posed a problem because, unlike the other provinces, it does not change its clocks to daylight saving time.

So while the polls close in the Eastern and Mountain time zones at 9:30 EDT, Saskatchewan's polling stations will stay open until 1O:30 EDT, making it impossible to publish nationwide results until then.
Broadcasters in particular are hit by the election rules. They face a jail term of up to two years if they are caught broadcasting election results in Saskatchewan before 10:30 EDT.
The rules also apply to the Internet, but at least two Internet providers have said they planned to circumvent the law.
